reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD & ACG
clinicalPearls: Almost always caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries, so patients typically have widespread vascular disease and risk factors such as smoking
The hallmark is postprandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina) beginning shortly after eating, leading to fear of food, reduced intake, and progressive weight loss

Because of the rich collateral circulation between the coeliac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries, symptoms usually require significant stenosis in more than one of the three main vessels
It is frequently underdiagnosed, and unexplained weight loss with food aversion in an arteriopath should prompt consideration of the diagnosis
CT or MR angiography, and duplex ultrasound, are used to demonstrate the arterial stenoses
Revascularisation, most often by endovascular angioplasty and stenting or by surgical bypass, relieves symptoms and prevents progression to acute intestinal infarction
Untreated disease can progress to acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction, a surgical emergency
Nutritional support and cardiovascular risk-factor modification are important adjuncts to revascularisation
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia develops when atherosclerotic stenosis of the splanchnic arteries limits the increase in blood flow required to meet the metabolic demand of the gut after meals. The resulting mismatch produces postprandial ischaemic pain. Because of extensive collateral pathways among the three main mesenteric arteries, symptomatic disease typically requires high-grade stenosis or occlusion of at least two vessels, or a critical single-vessel lesion where collaterals are inadequate. Chronic hypoperfusion impairs absorption and causes food avoidance and weight loss. Acute thrombosis superimposed on a stenosed vessel can precipitate acute mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction.
additionalDifferentials: Peptic ulcer disease and other upper GI causes of postprandial pain
Median arcuate ligament syndrome (coeliac axis compression)
additionalInvestigations: CT or MR angiography of the mesenteric vessels to demonstrate stenoses
Mesenteric duplex ultrasound as a non-invasive screening test
Catheter angiography when revascularisation is planned
Nutritional assessment given chronic weight loss
Exclusion of gastrointestinal malignancy and other causes of weight loss by endoscopy and imaging
redFlags: Sudden, severe, constant abdominal pain out of proportion to examination signalling acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia and bowel infarction
Rising lactate, acidosis, peritonism, or shock requiring emergency surgical evaluation
Rapid, marked weight loss with intractable food aversion
Progression of symptoms despite conservative measures indicating imminent vascular compromise
reference.prognosis: With timely revascularisation, symptoms usually resolve, weight is regained, and the risk of catastrophic bowel infarction falls. Untreated disease carries a substantial risk of progression to acute mesenteric ischaemia, which has high mortality. Overall outlook is also influenced by the patient's generalised atherosclerotic burden.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic postprandial pain and weight loss to malignancy or functional disease and missing a vascular cause
Failing to recognise that significant multi-vessel disease is usually needed to cause symptoms, leading to under-treatment of critical single-vessel lesions
Delaying revascularisation until acute infarction supervenes
Neglecting cardiovascular risk-factor management after treating the mesenteric lesions
